In hematoxylin-eosin staining, MCCs are dermal tumors composed of small, round, basophilic cells arranged in sheets or trabecular arrays (Figure 2). MCC cells have round, hyperchromatic nuclei with dusty (salt-and-pepper) chromatin, inconspicuous nucleoli, and scant cytoplasm with neuroendocrine granules (Figure 3). A high mitotic rate is frequent as well as vascular invasion and an abundant inflammatory infiltrate of lymphocytes and plasma cells surrounding the tumor. in_text_mentions: A definitive diagnosis of MCC is made on the basis of histopathology and immunohistochemistry. On hematoxylin and eosin examination, MCC is characterized by a proliferation of uniform, small, round, blue undifferentiated cells with spherical or oval nuclei and scant cytoplasm (Fig 3), high mitotic rate, apoptotic bodies, and occasional necrosis. In clinical practice, the most important immunohistopathologic features are dot-like positive CK-20 (Fig 4) and negative TTF-1 and CK-7 stainings.29

in_text_mentions: ositive with a paranuclear, cytoplasmic, or mixed pattern; chromogranin, synaptophysin, CD56, neuron-specific enolase (NSE) positive, but the pathognomonic clue is CK20 positivity with a classic dot-like paranuclear pattern. MCC cells are CK7, thyroid transcription factor (TTF)-1, CDX2, S100, CD45, and vimentin negative (Figure 2). Therefore, immunohistochemistry helps in distinguishing between MCC and other skin tumors such as basal cell carcinoma (CK20−), lymphoma (CD45+), small cell melanoma (S100+ CK20−), or metastatic neuroendocrine carcinoma (CD56+, synaptophysin+ TTF-1+, CK20−) [42,43].

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (a, b, c). a: Clinical photograph of an 82-year-old patient showing a classic presentation of Merkel cell carcinoma as a large, ulcerated reddish-livid cutaneous nodule with central erosions and hemorrhagic crusts above the right eyebrow, consistent with the described clinical features of MCC. b: Hematoxylin-eosin stained histopathology section from the patient's Merkel cell carcinoma lesion demonstrating the characteristic small round blue cell tumor morphology of MCC. c: Immunohistochemical staining of the patient's Merkel cell carcinoma lesion showing strong expression of MCPyV large T antigen in tumor cells, but this finding is not included in the provided vocabulary, so the panel does not meet inclusion criteria.

panels.figure_caption: Advanced Merkel cell carcinoma in an 82-year-old patient. MCC appears as pink to reddish-livid and sometimes skin-colored, often fast-growing, and painless, shiny nodules or plaques. The main features are described by the acronym AEIOU: asymptomatic, (rapidly) expanding nodules, immunosuppressed, older than 50 years, and UV radiation exposure [50]. (a) Merkel cell carcinoma above the right eye covering the eyebrow. Clinically, a large, ulcerated tumor nodule, between 3 and 4 cm in diameter, with central erosions and hemorrhagic crusts is seen. According to the patient, the tumor developed within a few months. (b) The histology of Merkel cell carcinoma is shown in (a). Proliferates of small to medium-sized, hyperchromatic, densely arranged, monomorphic basophilic cells with disrupted chromatin scaffolds and mitoses are seen (Hematoxylin-eosin stain, original magnification, 100:1). (c) Immunohistochemical staining with the anti-MCPyV large T-antigen mouse monoclonal antibody CM2B4 (Santa Cruz Biotechnology, Inc., Santa Cruz, California, United States, 200 µg/mL). Strong expression (brown stained cells) of the large T antigen in tumor cells is visible (original magnification, 100:1).
in_text_mentions: Clinical aspects of MCC are shown in Figure 3 and are described in the legend of the figure.

Clinical suspicion of MCC should be confirmed histologically and immuno-histochemically (Figure 3b,c), as the described features are nonspecific, and often MCC lesions are presumed to be benign in nature with differential diagnosis including cyst, lipoma, or folliculitis [46]. Early diagnosis and associated smaller tumor diameter and lower tumor stages are critical for the prognosis of MCC [47,48]. The latest developments in the diagnosis and treatment of MCC have been reviewed recently in this and other journals [49,50,51,52,53,54].

panels.figure_caption: Right-sided Merkel cell carcinoma of the temporal region in a 63-year-old male. The lesion started as a small violaceous nodule approximately six months prior to presentation. This was excised locally at an outside institution and subsequently recurred in the region of the previous excision. The lesion subsequently enlarged and resulted in right-sided weakness in the distribution of the frontal branch of the facial nerve. Pain in the region was mild. Subsequent biopsy revealed MCC. Note multinodular cutaneous induration and anterior violaceous appearance, classic for advanced MCC.
in_text_mentions: ontours where it is desirable to avoid excessive bulk. The reliable pedicle length and predictability of harvest make the radial forearm free flap a commonly utilized reconstructive technique for cutaneous defects of the head and neck. In cases with vessel-depleted necks where veins are unavailable, a semifree radial forearm harvest has been described dissecting the cephalic vein proximally and performing a single arterial anastomosis, which is unique to this flap [23]. Donor site morbidity is well tolerated, however generally inferior to the anterior thigh flap [24, 25] (Figures 2, 3, and 4).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: This is a representative H&E histopathology panel from a Merkel cell carcinoma case and visibly demonstrates the captioned small round blue cell morphology and crush artifact. B: This is a higher-magnification H&E view of the Merkel cell carcinoma showing the captioned small round cell tumor morphology and associated nuclear and mitotic features. C: The panel is a CK20 immunohistochemical stain from a case diagnosed as Merkel cell carcinoma, with the characteristic perinuclear dot-like pattern described in the caption and visible staining. D: This is a synaptophysin immunohistochemical panel from the same Merkel cell carcinoma case. The caption specifically describes characteristic hot-dots positivity, but this finding is not represented in the allowed vocabulary.

panels.figure_caption: Representative pictures of Merkel cell carcinoma. At a low magnification, nodular dermal-hypodermic neoplasia with small round blue cell appearance and crush artifact (A). At higher magnification, the neoplastic cells showed finely dispersed chromatin, indistinct nucleoli and scant cytoplasm with mitotic figures and apoptosis (B). The immunohistochemical study demonstrated characteristic CK20 (C) and synaptophysin “hot-dots” positivity (D), confirming the diagnosis. (A,B) Hematoxilyn-Eosin stain; original magnification: 20× for (A) and 200× for (B–D).
in_text_mentions: Biopsies were fixed in 10% formalin for 24 h, and paraffin-embedded 4 μm thick serial sections were stained with Hematoxylin and Eosin for a routine histopathological examination or were employed for immunohistochemistry. Immunostaining for CK20, CK7, TTF-1, synaptophyn and Ki67 was performed using a Leica Bond-III Immunostainer (Leica Biosystems, Milan, Italy). Tissue sections were deparaffinized and subjected to heat-induced epitope retrieval for 10 min at pH 9.0 (Figure 1).

At a low magnification, nodular dermal-hypodermic neoplasia with small round blue cell appearance and crush artifact (A). At higher magnification, the neoplastic cells showed finely dispersed chromatin, indistinct nucleoli and scant cytoplasm with mitotic figures and apoptosis (B). The immunohistochemical study demonstrated characteristic CK20 (C) and synaptophysin “hot-dots” positivity (D), confirming the diagnosis. (A,B) Hematoxilyn-Eosin stain; original magnification: 20× for (A) and 200× for (B–D).

in_text_mentions: PIEZO2 immunoreactivity was detected in all the cases, with a characteristic cytoplasmic pattern of distribution in the cells expressing CK20 (Figure 2a,b). The general pattern consisted in an overlap between membranous (Figure 2c–f and Figure 3a,b) and paranuclear dot-like (Figure 2g,h and Figure 3c,d) patterns.

panels.figure_caption: Single immunohistochemistry for CK20 (a,b), ChrA (c,d), Syn (e,f) and NFP (g,h) was used to characterize MCC cells. They showed two patterns of immunostaining: membranous perinuclear and dot-like. Scale bar 20 µm.
in_text_mentions: Merkel cells from human skin displayed immunoreactivity for CK20 and ChrA, which well co-localized with PIEZO2 (Figure S1). Structurally MCC formed cords, trabeculae or sheets of small monomorphic cells that occasionally contained blood vessels. The assessment and diagnosis of MCC was performed based on the expression of markers such as CK20 (Figure 1a,b), chromogranin A (Figure 1c,d), synaptophysin (Figure 1e,f) or NFP (Figure 1g,h), although the proportion of NFP positive cells was generally low.

panels.figure_caption: CK20 immunohistochemical staining of Case 1 (a, 20×), Case 2 (b, 20×), Case 3 (c, 100×; d, 200×), Case 4 (e, 40×; f, 200×), and Case 5 (g, 20×). Cases 1, 2, and 5 are negative for CK20, Case 3 is focally positive, and Case 4 demonstrates less than 5% positivity in the paranuclear dot‐like pattern. CK20: Cytokeratin 20.
in_text_mentions: cutaneous lesions and consisted of aggregates of small blue cells on H&E staining, as seen in Figure 1 and summarized in Table 1. On IHC staining, three of the cases were completely negative for CK20 (Figure 2), while two of the cases exhibited focal staining of CK20 (stained less than 5% of the total tumor), prompting additional testing. All five cases were negative for TTF‐1 but were strongly and diffusely positive for PanCK in the paranuclear dot‐like pattern (Figure 3), which supported the diagnosis of MCC in all instances. Other stains were variably obtained and are summarized in Table 1.

panels.attribution_text: García-Mesa et al. Merkel Cell Carcinoma Display PIEZO2 Immunoreactivity.. Journal of personalized medicine 2022. doi:10.3390/jpm12060894. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
panels.figure_caption: Immunofluorescence for PIEZO2, showing its two morphological patterns: cytoplasmic perinuclear (a,b) and dot-like pattern (c,d). Co-localization of PIEZO2 with CK20 (e) or ChrA (f) was regularly observed (merge in yellow). Arrow in ‘f’ indicates a ChrA+/PIEZO2− cell. The MCC cells were processed for simultaneous detection of PIEZO2 and NFP (g–j) only revealed a scarce number of cells showing co-localization of both (i), sometimes resembling MC-nerve contact (arrow in j). Scale bars 50 µm (a,c), 20 µm (b,d–j).
in_text_mentions: PIEZO2 immunoreactivity was detected in all the cases, with a characteristic cytoplasmic pattern of distribution in the cells expressing CK20 (Figure 2a,b). The general pattern consisted in an overlap between membranous (Figure 2c–f and Figure 3a,b) and paranuclear dot-like (Figure 2g,h and Figure 3c,d) patterns.

PIEZO2 immunoreactivity was also identified employing immunonofluorescence (Figure 3). Using double immunohistochemistry for PIEZO2 and CK20 (Figure 3e), PIEZO2 and ChrA (Figure 3f), or PIEZO2 and NFP (Figure 3g–j), we observed co-localization of those proteins in a variable proportion of cells within the tumor mass.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 6 panels (A, B, C, D, E, F). A: Human skin H&E section showing an MCC dermal tumor with subepidermal edema, basophilic tumor-cell nests and sheets, and dermal lymphatic invasion. B: Human skin H&E section demonstrating the described basophilic MCC tumor growth, with edema and lymphatic invasion. C: Higher-magnification human skin H&E image showing the small basophilic tumor cells characteristic of MCC, with collagen dissection and crush artifact described in the caption. D: CK20 immunohistochemistry shows the paranuclear dot-like staining pattern characteristic of Merkel cell carcinoma. E: Human MCC tissue with intact MLH1 nuclear staining and preserved internal controls, an ancillary immunohistochemical feature reported in the caption. F: Human MCC tissue with intact PMS2 nuclear staining and preserved internal controls, an ancillary immunohistochemical feature reported in the caption.

panels.figure_caption: In this example (A,B), subepidermal edema and dermal lymphatic invasion were evident. Uniform basophilic tumor cells formed nests and diffuse sheets surrounding the adnexal structures. Dissection of collagen and some crushing artifacts accompanied tumor cells (C). Paranuclear dot-like cytokeratin 20 stainings (D). MLH1 (E) and PMS2 (F) nuclear stainings were intact with internal controls. (Hematoxylin and Eosin stain, magnifications 40X [A, B], 200X [C], immunohistochemical stainings, magnifications 200X [CK20], 100X [MLH1, PMS2]).
in_text_mentions: There are two main pathogenic pathways for MCC development. In 2008, Chang, Moore, and colleagues found that 80% of MCC is associated with MCPyV (12). The other one, MCPyV negative, is related to UV exposure and a high mutation burden. Tumor protein p53 gene (TP53), retinoblastoma gene (RB) (13), and succinate dehydrogenase D gene (SDHD) mutations (14) are also involved in the molecular pathogenesis of Merkel cell carcinoma. Clinically it is a rapidly growing, painless, reddish-purplish nodule (15) (Figure 1). MCC diagnosis is based on histopathological examination in most cases (Figure 2).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: H&E stain showing classic small round blue cell morphology with basophilic cells, hyperchromatic nucleoli, and finely dispersed chromatin characteristic of Merkel cell carcinoma. B: Immunohistochemistry demonstrating the characteristic perinuclear dot-like CK20 staining pattern diagnostic for Merkel cell carcinoma. C: Immunohistochemistry showing diffuse chromogranin A positivity, confirming neuroendocrine differentiation in Merkel cell carcinoma. D: Immunohistochemistry demonstrating nuclear MCPyV (CM2B antibody) reactivity, confirming Merkel cell polyomavirus-associated Merkel cell carcinoma.

MCPyV DNA was detected by PCR and the major viral T-antigen was detected by nuclear positivity in immunohistochemistry using CM2B monoclonal antibody (Fig. 2D). panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Low-power H&E section from the reported Merkel cell carcinoma shows a diffusely infiltrative dermal tumor; the caption also explicitly identifies solar elastosis and superficial telangiectatic vessels. B: Higher-magnification H&E directly demonstrates the small round blue cell morphology characteristic of the Merkel cell carcinoma described in the article. C: The caption explicitly identifies positive AE1/AE3 immunostaining with focal paranuclear staining in the Merkel cell carcinoma. This is not labeled as CK20, so the CK20-specific vocabulary finding is not assigned.
panels.attribution_text: Alhaj et al. Merkel Cell Carcinoma on the Face: Case Report.. JMIR dermatology 2024. doi:10.2196/56658. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: (A) Lower power hematoxylin and eosin staining revealed skin with diffusely infiltrative tumor within the dermis. Prominent solar elastosis and telangiectatic blood vessels are seen in the superficial dermis. (B) On higher magnification, tumor cells can be seen to be composed of small round blue cells with a high nucleus to cytoplasm ratio, round/oval hyperchromatic nuclei with a finely stippled salt and pepper chromatic pattern, indistinct nuclei, and scant cytoplasm. Mitoses and apoptotic bodies are seen in between. Nuclear molding and crush artifacts are noted. (C) Positive cytokeratin (AE 1/AE 3) with focal paranuclear staining.
in_text_mentions: Immunohistochemistry markers confirmed the diagnosis of MCC and ruled out a metastatic deposit of small cell carcinoma of the lung. Histopathological features were also in favor of MCC. They are represented in Figure 2.

Prominent solar elastosis and telangiectatic blood vessels are seen in the superficial dermis. (B) On higher magnification, tumor cells can be seen to be composed of small round blue cells with a high nucleus to cytoplasm ratio, round/oval hyperchromatic nuclei with a finely stippled salt and pepper chromatic pattern, indistinct nuclei, and scant cytoplasm. Mitoses and apoptotic bodies are seen in between. Nuclear molding and crush artifacts are noted. (C) Positive cytokeratin (AE 1/AE 3) with focal paranuclear staining.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (a, b, c). a: Panel shows CK20 immunohistochemistry with characteristic perinuclear dot-like staining pattern diagnostic for Merkel cell carcinoma, as described in caption and confirmed in text. b: Panel shows synaptophysin immunohistochemistry with diffuse granular cytoplasmic expression, a neuroendocrine marker confirming Merkel cell carcinoma diagnosis as described in the article text. c: Panel shows chromogranin A immunohistochemistry with strong diffuse cytoplasmic positivity, a neuroendocrine marker confirming Merkel cell carcinoma diagnosis as described in the article text.
panels.attribution_text: Amoruso et al. Ultrasound Assessment in Merkel Cell Carcinoma: Case Report and Narrative Literature Review.. Reports (MDPI) 2026. doi:10.3390/reports9010043. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 6.
panels.figure_caption: Immunohistochemical staining (20×): (a) CK20: positive with perinuclear dot-like staining pattern. (b) Synaptophysin: diffuse granular cytoplasmic expression. (c) Chromogranin A: strong and diffuse cytoplasmic positivity.
in_text_mentions: Immunohistochemistry (IHC) demonstrated diffuse cytoplasmic positivity for synaptophysin, chromogranin A, CAM5.2, and CK20, which displayed the characteristic dot-like perinuclear staining pattern (Figure 6). Conversely, the lesion tested negative for CK7, TTF-1, S100, and p63. Testing for MCPyV was not performed. The Ki-67 proliferation index was 35–40%. These findings confirmed the diagnosis of MCC. The lesion was completely excised.

panels.rationale: Immunohistochemistry (CK20) from a cell block of malignant pleural effusion demonstrating the characteristic sharp perinuclear dot-like staining pattern pathognomonic for Merkel cell carcinoma. The article title and context confirm the diagnosis.
panels.attribution_text: Payne et al. Merkel cell carcinoma in a malignant pleural effusion: case report.. CytoJournal 2004. doi:10.1186/1742-6413-1-5. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: Cell block stained with CK20 demonstrating sharp perinuclear dot like pattern.
in_text_mentions: A year after first presenting for a right buttock mass, the patient was admitted to the hospital for increasing dyspnea. A chest radiograph revealed a large right pleural effusion, which was drained for both therapeutic and diagnostic purposes. The fluid was grossly bloody and cytology revealed abundant, round, basophilic single cells, many in mitosis, with characteristic granular, "salt and pepper" nuclear chromatin (Figure 1). A cellblock was made and immunohistochemical staining with CK20 revealed characteristic positivity in a dot like rim pattern (Figures 2).

plate_findings.evidence: CK20 immunostaining showing pathognomonic paranuclear dot pattern, exhibiting the characteristic perinuclear dotted staining pattern diagnostic of Merkel cell carcinoma.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (2a, 2b, 2c). 2a: IHC micrograph showing diffuse CD56 cytoplasmic positivity confirming neuroendocrine differentiation in Merkel cell carcinoma. 2b: IHC micrograph showing diffuse chromogranin A cytoplasmic positivity confirming neuroendocrine differentiation in Merkel cell carcinoma. 2c: IHC micrograph showing characteristic CK20 paranuclear dot-like staining pattern pathognomonic for Merkel cell carcinoma, distinguishing it from other small round blue cell tumors.
panels.attribution_text: Altamirano De La Cruz et al. Merkel Cell Carcinoma With Lymph Node Metastasis: A Case Emphasizing Early Diagnosis and Multidisciplinary Management.. Cureus 2025. doi:10.7759/cureus.90232. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: (a) Positive CD56 immunohistochemistry (neuroendocrine marker), 400×, demonstrating diffuse cytoplasmic staining confirming neuroendocrine differentiation of tumor cells. (b) Diffuse positive chromogranin A immunostaining, 400×, confirming neuroendocrine differentiation. Strong, diffuse cytoplasmic positivity throughout tumor cells is consistent with a neuroendocrine neoplasm. (c) CK20 immunostaining showing pathognomonic paranuclear dot pattern, 400×, exhibiting the characteristic perinuclear dotted staining pattern diagnostic of Merkel cell carcinoma. This distinctive paranuclear "dot-like" immunoreactivity is pathognomonic for MCC and distinguishes it from other small round blue cell tumors. Insert: High-power view demonstrating typical paranuclear dots.
in_text_mentions: demonstrated highly specific diagnostic findings. CK20 showed positive staining with the characteristic paranuclear pattern, highly specific for MCC. CD56 demonstrated diffusely positive cytoplasmic staining, indicating neuroendocrine differentiation. Chromogranin A exhibited diffusely positive, strong cytoplasmic staining, confirming neuroendocrine differentiation. Synaptophysin demonstrated diffusely positive cytoplasmic staining as an additional neuroendocrine marker. Ki-67 showed 80% positive nuclei, indicating a high proliferation index with significant prognostic implications (Figure 2).

Postoperative progression was favourable and the patient was discharged 5 days after surgery, with no complications. The final pathology report concluded that both lesions were consistent with metastatic MCC (Figure 3), with involvement of the serous membrane of the jejunal wall but no lymphovascular or perineural invasion. panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: IHC image from a patient's triphasic cutaneous carcinoma with Merkel cell features, showing pan-cytokeratin staining of epithelial tumor components and the trabecular architecture characteristic of the neuroendocrine Merkel cell component. B: IHC image from the same patient's tumor, demonstrating the pathognomonic dot-like paranuclear CK20 staining in the neuroendocrine component diagnostic for Merkel cell carcinoma. C: IHC image from the same patient's triphasic tumor, highlighting the squamous differentiation component via p40 positivity, a divergent lineage feature of this Merkel cell carcinoma case. D: IHC image from the same patient's triphasic tumor, highlighting the ductal differentiation component via CEA-poly staining, a divergent lineage feature of this Merkel cell carcinoma case.
panels.attribution_text: Khalil et al. Merkel Cell Carcinoma With Divergent Differentiation-Or Something Else? A Triphasic Cutaneous Carcinoma With Lineage Plasticity.. Journal of cutaneous pathology 2026. doi:10.1111/cup.70144. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
panels.figure_caption: Triphenotypic cutaneous carcinoma. Immunohistochemical findings supporting epithelial, neuroendocrine, and ductal differentiation. (A) Pan‐cytokeratin (AE1/AE3) immunohistochemical stain highlights epithelial differentiation and the distribution of the tumor components (AE1/AE3, 40×). (B) Cytokeratin 20 (CK20) immunohistochemical stain shows dot‐like paranuclear positivity in the neuroendocrine component, with absent staining in the sarcomatoid component (CK20, 400×). (C) p40 immunohistochemical stain highlights squamous differentiation, with negative staining in the sarcomatoid component (p40, 100×). (D) Polyclonal carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA‐poly) immunohistochemical stain highlights ductal differentiation and accentuates duct‐like structures (CEA‐poly, 400×).
in_text_mentions: d a well‐defined, firm mass measuring 2.7 × 2.3 × 0.8 cm. Histopathologic evaluation demonstrated a complex malignant neoplasm composed of three distinct but intimately admixed components (Figure 2). The first component consisted of nests and sheets of small basophilic cells with scant cytoplasm, finely granular (“salt‐and‐pepper”) chromatin, nuclear molding, frequent mitotic figures, and brisk apoptotic activity. This component showed dot‐like CK20 staining and strong expression of neuroendocrine markers, supporting a diagnosis of neuroendocrine carcinoma with Merkel cell features (Figure 3).

s, focal ductal lumina, and multifocal connection with an overlying carcinoma in situ. This component expressed high–molecular‐weight cytokeratins and p40, supporting squamous differentiation (Figure 3). Rare duct‐like structures were highlighted by EMA and polyclonal CEA, supporting focal ductal differentiation (Figure 3). Additional CK7 immunohistochemistry demonstrated staining in the squamoid/ductal epithelial component, further supporting adnexal ductal differentiation in this area (Figure 4). Although the morphology was not entirely classic for squamoid eccrine ductal carcinoma, the comb

The third component was composed of pleomorphic spindle and ovoid cells with marked cytologic atypia and abundant mitotic activity. This component lacked expression of epithelial and neuroendocrine markers, consistent with sarcomatoid dedifferentiation. Lymphovascular invasion was identified, and the microscopic margins were close. Immunohistochemical findings supporting the triphasic differentiation are summarized in Figure 3. The final integrated diagnosis was rendered as a carcinoma with Merkel cell features associated with squamous/ductal and sarcomatoid components.

in_text_mentions: An 80-year-old male patient with no relevant clinical history presented with an ulcerated, bleeding skin lesion on his left arm. Physical examination revealed a 2-cm raised, ulcerated lesion on the inner surface of the arm. A surgical resection was performed, and the histopathologic report confirmed MCC, with a tumor size of 1.5 cm and a thickness of 70 mm, exhibiting a nodular growth pattern and clear margins. Immunohistochemistry showed CK20 paranuclear dot-like staining and neuroendocrine features, including chromogranin and synaptophysin (Figure 1).

in_text_mentions: A definitive diagnosis of MCC is made on the basis of histopathology and immunohistochemistry. On hematoxylin and eosin examination, MCC is characterized by a proliferation of uniform, small, round, blue undifferentiated cells with spherical or oval nuclei and scant cytoplasm (Fig 3), high mitotic rate, apoptotic bodies, and occasional necrosis. In clinical practice, the most important immunohistopathologic features are dot-like positive CK-20 (Fig 4) and negative TTF-1 and CK-7 stainings.29

in_text_mentions: maternal breast cancer and stomach cancer in his 2 sisters. Physical examination revealed multiple painless and rapidly growing flesh-colored and red-violaceous nodules on the right axillary region (Fig. 1). in_text_mentions: During his initial examination, the dermatological assessment revealed a 24×23 mm dome-shaped, firm, red tumor with good mobility relative to the subcutaneous tissue (Figure 1A). Laboratory investigations showed mild renal impairment, an elevated HbA1c indicating poor glycemic control, and an increased level of neuron-specific enolase (NSE), a marker often elevated in neuroendocrine tumors. A PET-CT scan was conducted, which showed increased metabolic activity in the left upper arm but no evidence of distant metastasis, suggesting localized disease (Figure 1B).

Histopathological analysis of the excised tumor demonstrated nodular growths in the subcutaneous tissue, composed of cells with pale cytoplasms and inconspicuous nucleoli, a hallmark of MCC (Figure 1C). These cells densely proliferated without evidence of vascular or lymphatic invasion. Immunohistochemical staining was positive for CK20 in a characteristic dot-like pattern (Figure 1D), along with epithelial membrane antigen (EMA), chromogranin A, synaptophysin, and CD56, further supporting the diagnosis of MCC. Additionally, the presence of Merkel cell polyomavirus antibody was confirmed (Figu

rmed. Two months following intensive treatment with antiviral therapy, including remdesivir, and systemic corticosteroids, the patient rapidly developed in-transit metastasis along the path between the primary tumor site and the regional lymph nodes (Figure 1F). This complication led to additional surgical interventions and further radiotherapy. A second surgery was performed to address a local recurrence, with a 10 mm margin being taken. After the second surgery, adjuvant postoperative radiation therapy with 39 Gy (13 fractions), 3 Gy per fraction, using 6 MeV electron beams was administered.

in_text_mentions: The patient underwent wide local excision. Pathological examination confirmed a 14 cm ulcerated, infiltrative tumor with an estimated 60% necrosis, infiltrating the dermis and subcutaneous tissue. Histology showed a solid and nodular proliferation of monomorphic, medium-sized round cells with scant basophilic cytoplasm and finely stippled, non-nucleolated chromatin. The nearest lateral margin was uninvolved but immeasurably close, while the other margins ranged from 1 to 3.5 cm. No vascular emboli or perineural invasion were identified (Figure 2).

panels.figure_caption: Histopathological features (Hematoxylin & Eosin): (a) low-power view (4×) showing a nodular growth pattern. (b,c) Higher magnification (10× and 20×) showing dense proliferation of medium-sized monomorphic cells with oval nuclei, scant cytoplasm, and finely granular chromatin.
in_text_mentions: Microscopic analysis revealed an epithelial proliferation characterized by a nodular growth pattern, with solid clusters of cells separated by fibrous septa and focal areas of central necrosis. Cytologically, the neoplastic cells appeared monomorphic and medium-sized, exhibiting oval nuclei, scant cytoplasm, and the typical finely granular chromatin. The mitotic index was 10/mm2 (Figure 5).

in_text_mentions: A year after first presenting for a right buttock mass, the patient was admitted to the hospital for increasing dyspnea. A chest radiograph revealed a large right pleural effusion, which was drained for both therapeutic and diagnostic purposes. The fluid was grossly bloody and cytology revealed abundant, round, basophilic single cells, many in mitosis, with characteristic granular, "salt and pepper" nuclear chromatin (Figure 1). A cellblock was made and immunohistochemical staining with CK20 revealed characteristic positivity in a dot like rim pattern (Figures 2).

in_text_mentions: Dermoscopic evaluation demonstrated striking jewel-like clustered dark red-to-violaceous lacunae (well-demarcated, round-to-oval vascular spaces). plate_findings.evidence: violaceous, dome-shaped, ulcerated tumor on the left forearm
uniform small cells with high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio / nodular proliferation of small, round, hyperchromatic cells in the dermis

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Clinical photo of dome-shaped reddish-purple violaceous tumor on forearm with ulceration; caption and in-text confirm MCC diagnosis with CK20 perinuclear dot positivity. B: H&E histopathology showing small round hyperchromatic cells; in-text confirms nodular proliferation and CK20 perinuclear dot confirming MCC.
panels.attribution_text: Ohta et al. Case Report: Severe neutropenia induced by avelumab in a patient with Merkel cell carcinoma.. Frontiers in immunology 2025. doi:10.3389/fimmu.2025.1672282. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Clinical manifestation and histological examination. (A) Clinical image showing a violaceous, dome-shaped, ulcerated tumor on the left forearm. (B) Histopathologic examination revealed uniform small cells with high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio.
in_text_mentions: On physical examination, a dome-shaped, reddish-purple tumor measuring 37 × 32 mm was observed on the radial side of the left forearm ( Figure 1A ). The surface showed ulceration with necrotic crusts. The lesion was firm, broad-based, and not fixed to deeper structures. Blood tests revealed mildly elevated lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) (382 U/L) and neuron-specific enolase (NSE; 19.8 ng/mL). Computed tomography (CT) from the neck to pelvis revealed no distant metastasis.

down to the level of the fascia. A full-thickness skin graft was taken from the lower right abdomen and transplanted to the skin defect. Histopathology revealed a nodular proliferation of small, round, hyperchromatic cells in the dermis ( Figure 1B ). Immunohistochemical staining showed diffuse positivity for CK20 in a perinuclear dot-like pattern, confirming the diagnosis of MCC and excluding recurrence of follicular lymphoma. Tumor cells exhibited perineural invasion, with horizontal progression in subcutaneous tissue, indicating in-transit metastasis. Final staging was pT2pN2M0, stage IIA.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (a, b). a: Panel a shows left hemi-face at initial presentation with large red-violet multilobular cutaneous lesion; in-text confirms rapidly growing suborbital mass with histologically confirmed Merkel cell carcinoma. b: Panel b shows neck extension of same histologically confirmed Merkel cell carcinoma at initial presentation; caption and in-text state mass involving left hemi-face and extending to neck.
panels.attribution_text: Cerchiaro et al. Avelumab Treatment in Very Elderly People With Advanced Merkel Cell Carcinoma: A Case Report and Review of the Literature.. Cureus 2025. doi:10.7759/cureus.97683. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Patient at initial presentation (April 2024) (a) left hemi-face; (b) neck
in_text_mentions: A 95-year-old woman with no prior history of cancer presented in April 2024 with a rapidly growing suborbital mass involving her left hemi-face and extending to the neck (Figure 1). Histological examination confirmed Merkel cell carcinoma. MRI revealed a 6 cm multilobular hemorrhagic cutaneous lesion infiltrating the subcutaneous and periorbital soft tissues. She was partially dependent because of Parkinson's disease, but cognitively intact. No surgical or radiotherapeutic options were feasible due to the extent of disease and frailty.

panels.attribution_text: Berlingeri Collazo et al. panels.figure_caption: Positron emission tomography-computed tomography demonstrating increased fluorodeoxyglucose uptake within the right axillary region, corresponding to nodular soft tissue adjacent to surgical clips (arrow), initially interpreted as possible postoperative change but concerning for nodal disease
in_text_mentions: raphy demonstrated increased metabolic activity in the right axillary region, corresponding to nodular soft tissue measuring approximately 2.1 cm, with a maximum standardized uptake value of approximately 3.0 (Figure 1). This finding was initially interpreted as possibly related to postprocedural changes in the presence of surgical clips; however, nodal disease could not be excluded. Additional findings included a stable, enlarged pre-carinal lymph node measuring 1.2 cm with low-level fluorodeoxyglucose uptake and a 4-mm right lower lobe pulmonary nodule without significant metabolic activity.
